transcript:
Meeting header: 2026-12-22 16:00 UTC · 48 minutes · Recorded
Attendees: Alicia Moran (Redwood AE), Marco Li (Redwood SE), Naoko Sato (Redwood CSM), Priya Desai (BrightCart ML), Tom Reynolds (BrightCart Infra), Jamal Carter (BrightCart Head of ML), Leah Kim (BrightCart Product)
---
[00:00] Alicia Moran: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. Quick roll call. We wanted to focus today on the latest pilot numbers — quality deltas and latency tails — and sync on the next experiments. Marco, you want to kick us off with the perf summary?
[00:18] Marco Li: Yeah, sure. Quick context: we ran three variants over the last sprint — baseline fp16, int8 quantized, and an fp8 mix we called fp8-blend. Throughput wise, int8 gave about 1.9x token throughput on our bench, fp8-blend about 2.4x when kernels lined up, but the interesting part is the tail.
[00:36] Marco Li: p95 latency for int8 was roughly comparable to fp16 given batching, but p99 spiked more often — we saw spikes during KV cache rehydrates and when sequence lengths exceeded training distribution. Sometimes transcription shows "K-V cash" in logs but it's cache ops.
[00:55] Priya Desai: Sorry, can I ask — when you say "spikes" at p99, what's the magnitude? We're trying to map this to user-facing UI timeouts.
[01:05] Marco Li: Good call. On the small dedicated pool you sent, p95 ~ 210ms, p99 ~ 980ms for int8 in the worst runs; for fp8-blend p95 ~ 180ms, p99 ~ 620ms. Baseline fp16 p95 ~ 190ms, p99 ~ 420ms. So fp8 helped overall tails but had some variance depending on kernel selection and quantization fallback on long context.
[01:30] Tom Reynolds: Wait, that p99 jump on int8 — is that a memory pressure or kernel scheduling issue? Our infra team needs to know whether we should add headroom or avoid int8 in steady state.
[01:40] Marco Li: Mostly kernel fallbacks and recompile/alloctimes with the int8 path on longer sequences; also we observed a few runs where the model switched to a slower kernel for attention because of sequence alignment. We're tracking a kernel mismatch bug that can introduce an extra 200-400ms in some stacks.
[01:58] Priya Desai: That aligns with some hallucination spikes we saw last week. When the latency spiked, quality sometimes dipped — not huge, but measurable on our scoring. Did you see any systematic degradation on instruction-following?
[02:12] Marco Li: Yes — on our evaluation set, int8 had a mean SNR drop of about 1.8% on the PRF metric vs fp16, and fp8-blend had around 0.9% delta. But the more important is variance: some prompt clusters (long code completions, chain-of-thought) are more sensitive.
[02:30] Jamal Carter: So for production are we agreeing that fp8-blend is the sweet spot if we can manage kernel selection, but int8 is risky unless we gate by prompt type?
[02:40] Alicia Moran: That's a good binary. Our suggested playbook is prompt-class routing: sensitive prompts (code, long context, high-SLA flows) route to fp16 or fp8-precise, while high-throughput low-SLA flows can go to int8. Marco, we had promised a sensitivity sweep — status?
[02:57] Marco Li: We started it. So far 600 prompts sampled across the user buckets; early results show the sensitive cohort has up to a 4.5% quality regression on int8 in worst cases. We'll scale to 2k to get statistical power. That will also help produce a gating threshold for automatic routing.
[03:18] Priya Desai: 2k sounds good. We'll also send 500 product-specific prompts we worry about.
[03:25] Leah Kim: Quick Q: what about consistency over time? If we can tolerate a slight quality drop but it's stable, we can roll it more aggressively. If it's noisy then it's a showstopper.
[03:36] Marco Li: Right, stability matters. fp8-blend appears more stable in our experiments, less noisy across runs; int8 shows larger run-to-run variance. We suspect quantization granularity and per-layer scaling is causing the noise.
[03:50] Tom Reynolds: Can we avoid the kernel mismatch by pinning kernels or using a different runtime? Our infra team can accept a slight throughput reduction if it locks the kernel path.
[04:00] Marco Li: Yes, there's a runtime knob to prefer specific kernels and reduce dynamic recompile. That lowers throughput a bit but tightens p99. We can produce a recommended kernel profile for your dedicated pool.
[04:12] Priya Desai: On the hallucination front, how correlated were errors with tokens per second vs quantization? I want to know whether slowing down helps quality.
[04:22] Marco Li: Mostly correlated with quantization on a per-layer basis. Slowing down batching doesn't fix quantization noise; it helps tails by reducing scheduling contention. For hallucinations caused by numeric error, fp8/blend reduces them relative to int8.
[04:40] Alicia Moran: Wanted to surface a commercial ask: given these results, BrightCart asked for a short pilot extension to run the 2k sweep and a production-like gating experiment. We'll propose a 2-week extension with minimal incremental cost. I'll email terms.
[04:53] Jamal Carter: That's fine but we need predictable latency. If we add a fallback policy to route to fp16 when p99 exceeds threshold, that gives us safety.
[05:03] Marco Li: Agreed. We also propose automatic warm caches for prompts tagged as high-SLA and a prefix caching policy. That helps reduce rehydration. Some transcribes call it "pre cache" but it's prefix/KV cache.
[05:20] Tom Reynolds: Can Redwood give us an automation that adjusts routing dynamically per-route? For example, route 95% to int8 and keep 5% on fp8 for canary quality checks.
[05:30] Marco Li: Yes, we have a rollout policy that supports traffic splitting by route/model/variant and can fallback by quality gates. We can configure it to keep a shadow sample to compare outputs and trigger rollback if delta exceeds X.
[05:44] Priya Desai: Important: we need the exact math for the quality gating — what metric, window size, and thresholds? Our SLO is 99.5% success for our chat assistant and p99 under 800ms ideally.
[05:57] Marco Li: For gating we recommend using a composite metric — weighted PRF + user-acceptable diff threshold. Practically we'll start with PRF delta <= 1.5% over a 1k sample window and p99 latency <= 800ms. But that's configurable.
[06:15] Leah Kim: If we set PRF delta threshold tighter, can we still get meaningful cost savings?
[06:21] Marco Li: Yes, with smarter batching and prefix caching you'll recover most of the delta. We can also use a hybrid: fp8 for long-context heavy prompts, int8 for short answers. That preserves quality where needed.
[06:35] Alicia Moran: Okay, let's get into the plan items. Marco, outline the sweep and deliverables.
[06:42] Marco Li: Sweep plan: run 2k prompt set (1k representative + 1k customer-supplied). For each prompt we record: token latency, model variant, PRF score, temperature, sequence length, kernel used. We'll produce a CSV and delta tables. Expect raw output and summary charts. We'll also run a small canary routing test in your dedicated pool: 10% traffic to int8 and 10% shadowed to fp8 for comparison over 24 hours.
[07:07] Priya Desai: Shadowing is great. Do you need any infra changes for the 10% canary?
[07:13] Tom Reynolds: We can do traffic split on our side if we get instructions. We have autoscaling and the dedicated pool, but need the exact deployment manifest if kernel pinning is required.
[07:24] Marco Li: We'll provide a recommended manifest and the kernel pin profile. Also provide a lightweight script to extract p95/p99 by endpoint.
[07:32] Alicia Moran: Naoko, can you attach the security addendum and the kernel notes to the follow-up email?
[07:37] Naoko Sato: Yup, I'll include the security whitepaper, SOC2 summary, and a short runbook on kernel pins and fallback policies.
[07:44] Priya Desai: On the quality scoring, can you share your evaluation harness? We want to run the same PRF locally for parity.
[07:51] Marco Li: We'll share the eval harness (small python repo) and the seed scripts so you can reproduce metrics. Beware some infra-specific metrics may vary because of different runtimes.
[07:59] Jamal Carter: One risk I want to call out: vendor variance. If we switch vendors for dedicated hardware later, calibration may change. Is the gating approach portable?
[08:09] Marco Li: The gating logic is model-agnostic; quantization parameters require re-calibration per hardware and kernel. The playbook will call out a re-calibration step when moving hardware.
[08:19] Priya Desai: Any competitor concerns? We've heard from our procurement team that Anthropic offers some bounded-int precision endpoints — are they any easier to manage?
[08:29] Alicia Moran: Short answer: every provider has tradeoffs. Anthropic/OpenAI have managed endpoints but less control over routing and private dedicated pools. That's where Redwood's routing and kernel tuning add value. We can share comparative notes.
[08:41] Tom Reynolds: Cost question: assuming we use fp8-blend for 50% of traffic and int8 for 40%, fp16 for 10% sensitive, what's the expected token cost reduction?
[08:53] Marco Li: Roughly 45-60% unit cost reduction depending on batch sizes. We'll provide a cost model spreadsheet with scenarios.
[09:03] Priya Desai: Great. Anything else on regressions? We had a small regression on JSON output formatting in one int8 run last week. Is that expected?
[09:13] Marco Li: That's likely quantization noise near tokenization boundaries; we saw that in a few examples. The mitigation is blending or post-process rerank/filter for structured outputs. We'll flag structured-output prompts to route conservatively.
[09:27] Alicia Moran: Let's capture the explicit next steps: Marco runs the 2k sweep and provides CSV, Alicia sends pricing and pilot extension, Priya sends 500 prompts, Tom sends perf logs. Naoko will send security notes and kernel runbook. Any objections?
[09:45] Jamal Carter: No objections — sounds good.
[09:48] Priya Desai: One last ask: can we add a short shared dashboard that shows the p95/p99 and PRF deltas in near real-time during the canary?
[09:58] Marco Li: Yep, we can spin up a temporary dashboard and grant read access. We'll wire it to your metrics export.
[10:06] Alicia Moran: Perfect. We'll reconvene next Tuesday same time for results readout. Thanks everyone.
[10:12] End meeting.
